deep.reconstruction:
Context. In §§40–61 Euler builds a one-dimensional theory of steady outflow through a vertical tube BC. The tube has length b and width g (cross-section gg) and hangs below a reservoir of section ff and height AB = a; the outlet section is kk. His friction hypothesis is Coulomb-like: the wall friction on an element is proportional to the local absolute pressure, which includes the atmospheric head l, with coefficient α, per unit tube width g. Integrating the momentum balance along the tube therefore produces exponential factors e^{±αb/g}. The velocity head v is a fraction. Its numerator contains terms 𝔄 (from the reservoir) and 𝔅g − l, where 𝔅 = (1 − e^{−αb/g})/α. The denominator contains 1 − k⁴/f⁴-type terms, which Euler dropped in §45 by assuming a wide reservoir.

§62. Euler poses a test case. Let the upper vessel become infinitely narrow (ff → 0), so the tube is effectively closed at the top. Experience says water then does not run out through CC unless the tube is very long. In fact this is the Torricelli/barometer effect: the column must exceed about one atmosphere of water head. Euler notes that his frictionless formula, with the k⁴/f⁴ term already dropped, does not give v = 0 when f = 0.

§63. With friction, f = 0 gives 𝔄 = 0, so the numerator reduces to (1 − e^{−αb/g})g/α − l. He says the denominator need not be considered: it would contain k⁴/f⁴ = ∞, a term omitted in §45. No outflow occurs when 1 − e^{−αb/g} < αl/g, i.e. e^{−αb/g} > 1 − αl/g. Expanding the exponential gives the equivalent condition l > b − αb²/(2g) + α²b³/(6g²) − … . Inverting with the logarithm, there is no outflow when αb/g < −ln(1 − αl/g), i.e.
 b < −(g/α) ln(1 − αl/g) = l + αl²/(2g) + α²l³/(3g²) + α³l⁴/(4g³) + … .
So the critical tube length exceeds the barometric water head l by a friction correction, and it reduces to b = l as α → 0. This recovers the classical hydrostatic threshold in the frictionless limit.

§64. Numerical example (completed on the next page): α = 1/4000, a = 1/3 ft, b = 4 ft, gg = 1/2500 ft² (g = 1/50 ft), outlet fully open (kk = gg). Then αb/g = 1/20 and e^{1/20} − 1 = 0.05127. The next page's value g/α − l = 50 implies l = 30 ft. The result is v = 1/3 + 50·0.05127 = 2.896 ft, against a + b = 4⅓ ft without friction. Euler proposes calibrating α by measuring discharge.
errors: In the series step Euler (or the printer) writes '1 − αb/g + α²b²/2g² − α³b³/6g³ etc. < 1 − αl/g'. It follows from e^{−αb/g} > 1 − αl/g, so the sign must be '>'. The next deduction, 'l > b − αbb/2g + …', is nevertheless correct.
The series in 'l > b − αbb/2g + α²b³/6gg etc.' implicitly continues with alternating signs (the expansion of (g/α)(1 − e^{−αb/g})); this is fine but only implied by 'etc.'.

Physically the friction law is wrong: friction is taken proportional to absolute pressure, including atmospheric pressure. The real cause of the phenomenon is that the pressure at the closed top would become negative, so a void forms or the column breaks, when b < l. Euler's α-correction to the threshold has no physical basis. He himself remarks that the phenomenon is 'otherwise very easy to explain'. The failure of the frictionless formula comes from his own dropping of the k⁴/f⁴ term, since keeping it would make v → 0 as f → 0. It is not a defect of frictionless theory as such.
Housekeeping: the next page is numbered 352 in the transcription but should be 362.

ideas.what: Threshold condition for no outflow from a top-closed tube, derived from the numerator of the discharge formula: b < −(g/α) ln(1 − αl/g).
ideas.modern_name: Barometric (Torricelli) limit for a liquid column, with a spurious pressure-dependent friction correction
ideas.usually_credited_to: Torricelli/Pascal for the hydrostatic limit; the friction version is Euler's own (E260)
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 6 (1756/57, publ. 1761); Opera omnia II.13 (unsure of exact volume)

ideas.what: Inverting an exponential inequality via the logarithmic series −ln(1 − x) = Σ xⁿ/n.
Friction in a fluid proportional to normal pressure (Coulomb/Amontons-type law applied to fluids), producing an exponential pressure decay along the pipe.
ideas.modern_name: Early pipe-friction model, superseded by Darcy–Weisbach / Poiseuille viscous laws
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E260); later correct laws by Chézy, Prony, Hagen, Poiseuille, Darcy
ideas.where_published: E260; discussed in Truesdell's historical introductions to Euler's fluid mechanics (unsure of exact location)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine application of Euler's (physically incorrect) pressure-proportional friction model to a limiting case, with standard series manipulations. E260 is known and catalogued, and nothing here appears unrecorded or of modern interest beyond the history of erroneous friction hypotheses.
transcription_corrections: 'fractionem k⁴/f⁴ = f' should almost certainly read 'k⁴/f⁴ = ∞', since with f = 0 the fraction is infinite.
In the series line, the printed inequality sign before '1 − αl/g' should be '>' as a matter of mathematics, whatever the print shows.
